title: The thermal lever against the duplicate-cell floor: how large a temperature spread a lifetime divergence needs, and how large a module offers
description: Pre-registered calculation of how large a steady temperature difference between nominally identical lithium-ion cells two published temperature-dependent ageing laws need to produce a lifetime difference as large as the duplicate-cell floor of the Geslin et al. dynamic-cycling dataset (mean 3.0 %, 95th percentile 8.7 %, worst of eight 4.1 % at 90 % state of health), and how large a temperature difference a module at 35 C offers: an eight-cell lumped network of LG M50 21700 cells and a resolved scikit-fem cell, at average rates from C/16 to 2C and convection coefficients of 5, 10 and 25 W/(m2 K). Predictions were committed and pushed before any lever or spread was computed. At 35 C the LiFePO4 law of Schimpe et al. 2018 needs 1.68 K for the 95th percentile; the NCA+LNO / Si-graphite law of Kucinskis et al. 2022, the closest published match found to the dataset's cells, peaks near 35 C, so its lever there is weak and of undetermined sign (its registered slope needs 8.8 K of the opposite sign). With constant-current heat at the dataset's average rates (C/16 to C/2) the module offers at most 0.39 K between cells and a resolved cell 0.09 K inside itself, an implied lifetime divergence below the 3.0 % mean floor under both laws; a post-hoc estimate with the dataset's own published discharge-current variance and its CC-CV charge puts six of its eight dynamic C/2 protocols at 3.5 to 6.1 % under the LiFePO4 law (h = 10 W/(m2 K)), above the mean floor, while the NCA law's registered slope keeps every protocol below 1.2 %. An independent recomputation and the reports of two further independent checks are included. Code under the MIT licence; results, figure and note under CC BY 4.0. Version 1.1.0 adds Stage 2, which measures the lever on the KIT ageing dataset of Luh and Blank (LG INR18650HG2, twelve protocols at 0, 10, 25 and 40 C, three cells each, doi:10.35097/1969), with eight predictions committed and pushed before any cell value was read: from 25 to 40 C the lever runs from -3.45 to +1.91 % per K by protocol (positive at a 0.33 C charge in five of six protocols, negative at 1C and faster), negative from 10 to 25 C in every protocol; the dataset's replicate floor is 7.3 % (mean) and 20.5 % (95th percentile) at 90 %, larger than the Geslin floor; the warmer replicate reached 90 % first in 40 % of 142 pairs; and Stage 1's 0.391 K module offer implies at most 1.35 % divergence. Five of the eight predictions held. Version 1.2.0 adds Stage 3, which measures the lever in a second laboratory's data: the Sandia National Laboratories cycling study of Preger et al. 2020 (doi:10.1149/1945-7111/abae37; 86 commercial 18650 cells, LFP, NCA and NMC, cycled at 15, 25 and 35 C; files shared on request by Battery Archive, www.batteryarchive.org), with ten predictions committed and pushed before any lifetime or temperature value was computed. Structure checks before any result found records logged out of cycle order in every 35 C cell and, in most of them, counters that restart on the last sample of a discharge, so that the registered ampere-hour rule would have counted under 3 % of the LFP cells' discharge at 35 C; the correction was recorded and pushed before computing. On the registered 1C series, between the logged cell temperatures, the lifetime to 90 % rises from 25 to 35 C for NMC (s = -2.4 % per K; the KIT cell, inside its KIT band at a 1C discharge) and for NCA (-2.0 % per K); from 15 to 25 C s is -5.6 % per K for NMC, -1.3 for NCA and +3.4 for LFP (at 95 %). LFP's 25 to 35 C lever is not determinable as registered, because one 35 C cell logged no cell temperature before its lifetime (post hoc about +13 % per K). The capacity checks lie 60 to 470 equivalent full cycles apart, so 59 of 60 replicate pairs are tied within the check spacing and the replicate floor (mean 11 to 37 % by chemistry) measures the spacing as much as the cells. Stage 1's 0.391 K module offer moves NCA lifetimes by 0.8 %. Four of the ten predictions held, four did not and two were not scored. An independent recomputation by a separate checker, written from the decisions and the raw files without the pipeline's code, reproduces every per-cell value, the levers with their intervals, the floor and the thermal share to 7e-13, and all ten verdicts. The raw files are not redistributed; per-cell derived values are included with the citation. Version 1.3.0 adds Stage 4, which runs the measured levers through Stage 1's module and sizes the experiment that would settle the question, with seven predictions committed and pushed before any Stage 4 computation. The eight-cell LG M50 module is solved at 35, 25 and 10 C ambient, at C/4 to 2C and h = 5, 10 and 25 W/(m2 K), each cell's heat from the resistance that Stage 1's PyBaMM procedure (DFN, ORegan2022 parameters) gives at the ambient: 18.7, 26.6 and 47.9 mOhm. Under the median of each band's measured levers (25 to 40 C: twelve KIT protocols and the Sandia NMC value, median 1.30 % per K; 10 to 25 C: twelve KIT protocols and three Sandia chemistries, 3.58 % per K), the module's implied lifetime divergence, |s| times its cell-to-cell spread, exceeds the 3.0 % Geslin mean floor at 35 C only at 2C (6.2 to 7.0 %) and its 8.7 % 95th percentile at no rate up to 2C; at 10 C ambient it exceeds the mean floor from C/2 and the 95th percentile from 1C. The registered heat takes the resistance at the ambient and is an upper bracket: with each cell's heat at its own, warmer temperature (post hoc) the 1C divergence in 10 C air falls to 5.5 to 7.3 %, below the 95th percentile, and two failed predictions would hold and one held prediction fail. A paired t-test of log lifetimes with the floor's pair difference as log-normal noise, at 5 % and 80 % power, needs 3 duplicate pairs held 5 K apart in a 10 C chamber and 25 pairs held 2 K apart in a 35 C chamber against the Geslin floor (5 and 128 against the KIT floor). Four of the seven predictions held. Checks reproduce Stage 1's module bitwise, rederive the resistance by separate code within 0.02 %, recompute two cases by hand, and simulate the power calculation, which overstates the pairs needed by up to 25 % at small n under the log-normal floor. An independent recomputation by a separate checker, written from the decisions and the inputs before it opened any Stage 4 result, agrees to 2e-12 with the same seven verdicts. Version 1.4.0 adds Stage 5, which tests whether the lever is local: the replicate cells of one set sat at slightly different temperatures, and Stage 5 asks whether their lifetime differences follow the between-set lever times their temperature difference, with eight predictions committed and pushed before any Stage 5 computation. Over the 106 KIT replicate pairs whose set has a measured lever (0.44 K root mean square apart), the within-set log-lifetime difference recovers -0.09 times the between-set prediction (95 % interval by resampling sets: -2.05 to +1.37), so neither the between-set lever nor its absence is resolved, and the sign agrees in 45 of 106 pairs. The 56 Sandia pairs give 1.55 (-0.74 to +2.50), but they are ordered by Stage 3's within-cycle swing, a cell's own heat, which is no evidence of a thermal lever. These replicates could not have shown it: 104 of the 106 KIT pairs and all 56 Sandia pairs differ by less than their check spacing, their residual spread is the KIT duplicate floor, and the smallest lever they could detect at 80 % power is 6.6 % per K, 5.0 and 1.8 times the median warm and cold between-set levers; at the warm band's 0.35 K spread the warm median would need 4,221 replicate pairs, against 128 held 2 K apart in Stage 4's chamber experiment. Six of the eight predictions held. Checks reproduce the archived inputs bitwise, recompute every slope with separate code and a second random generator, recompute two pairs by hand and simulate the power calculation; INDEPENDENT_ZENODO_PLACEHOLDER
